title: Marx v. Department of Commerce
lead: Birch Lane appeared as public land on a 1911 subdivision plat but remained undeveloped by local authorities. Decades later, neighboring owners sought to vacate the dedication, and the township’s attempted acceptance proved too late under both lapse and affirmative-withdrawal principles.

actors.name: George and Laura Franklin
actors.role: Owners who platted Zenith Heights and dedicated streets in 1911.

actors.name: Raymond and Jean Marx
actors.role: Later lot owners seeking vacation of Birch Lane and quiet title.

actors.name: Bay Township
actors.role: Local authority relying on plat approval and a 1979 resolution.

actors.name: Charlevoix County road commission
actors.role: Authority asserting earlier acceptance and road jurisdiction.

actors.name: Judge O’Connell
actors.role: Author of the Michigan Court of Appeals opinion.

proceedings: The trial court granted summary disposition to the Marxes and vacated the dedication. The township and road commission appealed; the Court of Appeals affirmed because no timely manifest acceptance was shown and the offer had lapsed and been withdrawn.
limits: The decision recognizes informal as well as formal acceptance and does not establish a universal sixty-eight-year cutoff. Authority to accept, road-end theories, and broad lake-access policy were not decided on their merits. The report’s acquisition and driveway dates are retained without inventing a reconciled construction history.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A recorded subdivision offers Birch Lane for public use
sections.cue: What later private property lay beside it?
paragraphs: In August 1911, George and Laura Franklin platted Zenith Heights in Bay Township, Charlevoix County, designating streets and alleys for public use. Birch Lane ran between Lots six and seven from Valley Brook Avenue to Walloon Lake. The township approved the plat August 14.

Raymond and Jean Marx acquired Lot six in 1970, Lot seven in 1976, and Lot five in 1977. The factual narrative placed their residence on Lot seven and described a driveway encroaching on Birch Lane. The later withdrawal analysis dated the driveway to 1970. In 1993, the Marxes sought vacation of the dedication and a declaration quieting title, alleging that neither township nor road commission had accepted it.

sections.title: The public authorities offer several theories of acceptance
sections.cue: How did summary disposition reach the appellate court?
paragraphs: The government defendants sought summary disposition under Michigan Court Rule 2.116(C)(10), relying on plat approval, asserted maintenance expenditure, and an alleged assumption of jurisdiction under the McNitt Act. The owners requested judgment under Rule 2.116(I)(2), arguing no acceptance and private conduct withdrawing the offer.

The trial court ruled for the owners and ordered vacation. Although others, including the Department of Commerce, were named, only Bay Township and the road commission pursued the consolidated appeals. Judge O’Connell wrote for Judges Fitzgerald and assigned circuit judge T. L. Ludington, reviewing anew whether documents created a genuine material factual issue and who was entitled to judgment.

sections.title: The McNitt materials do not identify an accepted Birch Lane dedication
sections.cue: Why were the map and mileage survey insufficient?
paragraphs: The road commission relied on the McNitt Act, repealed in 1951, which directed staged incorporation of township highway mileage and then dedicated roads in specified recorded plats. It found no resolution assuming Birch Lane’s jurisdiction, offering only a purported McNitt map and a 1938 certified subdivision-mileage survey.

Kraus, an earlier dedication decision, required identification of the road or plat; even a general resolution claiming all township roads did not manifest knowing acceptance. Otherwise an authority could acquire unwanted duties and expenses. Here there was not even that general resolution. The map neither referred to Birch Lane nor explained its purpose, and the survey omitted its mileage and any demonstrated McNitt connection. Neither supported acceptance of this lane.

sections.title: A public dedication requires a manifest act beyond the proprietor’s offer
sections.cue: Why did plat approval and discussion of improvements fail?
paragraphs: A valid dedication required the recorded manifestation of the proprietor’s intent and timely acceptance by the proper authority. Acceptance could be formal or arise through qualifying public opening, improvement, regulation, expenditure, or use. It protected authorities against obligations for unwanted land. The authority bore the acceptance burden; the owner bore withdrawal. A completed timely dedication could also limit judicial vacation without official consent.

Although Subdivision Control Act §253(1) described recording as a fee-simple conveyance for designated uses, precedent still required acceptance. The court did not make a formal resolution the exclusive method.

Earlier panels differed on plat approval alone: Bangle treated it as acceptance, Salzer did not. This panel adopted Salzer because approval without reference to accepting the dedicated property lacked the necessary manifestation, consistent with Kraus. Richey, concerning a different Zenith Heights road frequently used for traffic, did not establish blanket acceptance of every platted street.
The record also showed a 1952 discussion of financing improvements to roads including Birch Lane, but no actual work or expenditure there. Discussion of possible action was not acceptance.

sections.title: The 1979 resolution is sufficient in form but arrives after unreasonable delay
sections.cue: How did the court assess lapse?
paragraphs: The township’s 1979 resolution accepting previously unaccepted dedicated lands specifically named Zenith Heights. Assuming township authority, it ordinarily satisfied the form of acceptance. The commission argued at oral argument that only it could accept, but failed to brief the issue; the court treated it as abandoned and did not decide which body possessed the power.

An unwithdrawn dedication offer could continue, but circumstances controlled its duration. The court compared cases finding eighty-six and eighty-seven years unreasonable with one it described as allowing twenty-six. Sixty-eight years here resembled the former. The township showed no intent to hold the offer open indefinitely, and three generations was unreasonable on this record. The offer had therefore lapsed before the resolution. That was contextual, not a fixed statutory sixty-eight-year limit.

sections.title: Affirmative private use supplies an independent withdrawal ground
paragraphs: Withdrawal required conduct inconsistent with public ownership, assessed with its nature and government acquiescence. Other cases involved structures, fences, trees, and underbrush. The Marxes supplied unrefuted evidence of a driveway on Birch Lane built in 1970 and of the commission telling them the township did not intend to develop the road.

They regularly parked there and treated the strip as private property. Complete blockage was unnecessary merely because one prior case had involved it. These affirmative uses, together with public acquiescence, withdrew the offer independently of lapse through delay.

A 1978 statutory acceptance presumption did not save the dedication. Section 255b(2)(a) permitted rebuttal by competent evidence of withdrawal before the statute took effect and before acceptance. The court placed withdrawal in 1970, preceding both the statute and the 1979 attempt.

sections.title: The vacation order stands without deciding every public-access issue
sections.cue: What did the final judgment leave open?
paragraphs: The court declined road-end access issues unnecessary to the result. A general public-policy argument favoring lake access was abandoned because it was omitted from the statement of questions and lacked pertinent authority. Those were not merits rulings against public lake access.

On November 12, 1996, the Court of Appeals affirmed summary disposition and vacation of Birch Lane’s dedication. No trial or further evidence was ordered, no contract damages were awarded, and no general right to close all road ends was announced. No separate opinion appeared.
